passages.t: Not one stone left on another
passages.happening: Jesus is leaving the temple for the last time in Mark. One of his disciples looks up at the walls and says, “Teacher, look at the magnificent stones and buildings!” Jesus answers that every one of those stones will be thrown down. Later they sit on the Mount of Olives, a hill just east of the city, looking across the valley at the temple. Four of the disciples, Peter, James, John, and Andrew, ask him quietly two questions. When will this happen? And what sign will tell them it is about to happen?
passages.hearers:
The disciple was not wrong to be impressed. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 or 19 BC, and work on the courts went on for decades after his death. The Jewish historian Josephus, who saw it, wrote that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow, because the stone was so white, and that parts of it were covered with gold (Jewish War 5.222-223). Some of the great blocks can still be seen today in the walls around the Temple Mount.

So Jesus' words would have sounded almost unthinkable. This was the house of God, the center of Jewish life, and it looked as if it would stand forever.

Yet within about forty years it was gone. The Jewish revolt against Rome began in AD 66. In AD 70 a Roman army under Titus took Jerusalem, and the temple burned. In Rome the Arch of Titus, built around AD 81, still shows soldiers carrying the temple's great lampstand in a victory parade.
passages.ot: Jesus was not the first Jew to say the temple would fall. Centuries earlier the prophet Micah had said, “Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble” (Micah 3:12), and Jeremiah warned the people not to trust in the building as if it made them safe (Jeremiah 7:4). The first temple, built by Solomon, was destroyed by Babylon. Jesus speaks in the line of those prophets. He speaks from inside Israel, with grief, and not as an enemy.
passages.hard: Was this a prophecy, or was it written after the event? Some scholars think Mark wrote his Gospel after AD 70, so the words could reflect what had already happened. Others note that Mark gives none of the details of the siege, such as the fire, and think he wrote shortly before it, in the 60s. Both views are held by careful readers. Either way, a prophet saying the temple would fall was not new in Israel, as Micah and Jeremiah show.
passages.asks: The disciple looked at the stones and felt safe. Jesus looked at the same stones and saw how short their life was. Ask what in your life looks permanent: a job, a church building, a country, your own strength. Jesus does not ask you to despise those things. He asks you not to rest your whole weight on them.

passages.happening: Jesus does not begin with a date or a sign. He begins with a warning: “See to it that no one deceives you.” Many will come claiming to be him. There will be wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes and famines. But do not be alarmed, he says. The end is not yet. These are only the beginning of birth pains. Then he turns to the disciples themselves. They will be handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues, and made to stand before governors and kings. The good news must first be preached to all the nations. When they are arrested, the Holy Spirit will give them words. Families will turn against each other. They will be hated because of his name, but the one who endures to the end will be saved.
passages.hearers:
Mark's first readers did not need to imagine any of this. In the years after Jesus, men rose up in Judea promising signs of rescue. Josephus tells of one named Theudas, who around AD 45 promised to part the Jordan River, and of a prophet from Egypt who gathered people on the Mount of Olives and said Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.97-98 and 20.169-172). The book of Acts mentions both men (Acts 5:36 and 21:38). Roman soldiers scattered both movements.

The warnings about councils and governors also fit what happened to the first Christians. Acts tells of apostles beaten by the council in Jerusalem (Acts 5:40) and of Paul standing before governors and a king (Acts 24 to 26).

Birth pains were a picture the prophets used. Labor pain is real, and once it begins it cannot be stopped. But it is the pain of something being born. Jesus is saying that the troubles are real and hard, and that they are not the end of the story.
passages.ot:
Isaiah used this same picture for Israel's suffering before God's rescue: “As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain” (Isaiah 26:17).

The split inside families echoes the prophet Micah, who mourned a time when “a man's enemies are the members of his own household” (Micah 7:6).
passages.hard:
Every age has had wars, earthquakes, and famines, and in every age someone has said they prove the end is here. Jesus says the opposite. These things “must happen, but the end is still to come.” They are not a countdown. They are the normal weather of a broken world, and Jesus tells his followers not to be alarmed by them.

Verse 12 speaks of family members betraying each other. That is a painful verse for anyone who has been hurt by their own family, whether for their faith or for some other reason. Jesus names that pain honestly. He does not call it good. He promises that those who endure it are not forgotten.
passages.asks: The first danger Jesus names is not war. It is being fooled. Ask who you let tell you what the news means, and whether fear makes you easier to fool. Jesus also says that when his people are dragged into court, it becomes a chance to speak about him. Where might a hard place in your life become a place to bear witness?

passages.happening: Jesus gives a sign at last. When they see “the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be,” those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. Do not go back into the house for anything. Do not go back from the field for your coat. It will be terribly hard for women who are pregnant or nursing. Pray that it does not happen in winter. Those days will bring distress worse than any before, and God will cut them short for the sake of his chosen people. Then he warns again: false Christs and false prophets will come with signs and wonders. Do not believe them. “I have told you everything in advance.”
passages.hearers:
An abomination is something disgusting to God, usually an idol. The phrase ‘the abomination of desolation’ means a horrible thing that leaves the holy place empty and ruined. Jesus' hearers knew where it came from: the book of Daniel.

They also knew what it had meant once before. Around 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple in Jerusalem. The Jewish book of 1 Maccabees calls it by this very name (1 Maccabees 1:54). Faithful Jews fled to the hills. More recently, around AD 40, the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself set up in the temple. Crowds of Jews said they would rather die. The order was delayed, and Caligula was murdered in January 41 before it was carried out. So the phrase pointed to a real fear that had nearly come true in living memory.

Notice the small aside, ‘let the reader understand’. Most early Christians heard the Gospels read aloud. Mark seems to be nudging the one reading, and everyone listening: think hard about this.

The details fit Judea. Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, so a man on the roof could run without going inside. A field worker left his cloak at the edge of the field. In winter, heavy rain flooded the dry stream beds and made escape on foot hard.

The church historian Eusebius, writing in the early 300s, reports that the Christians of Jerusalem were warned and left the city before the war, settling at Pella, east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Historians debate how much of that story is history. But it shows that early Christians took this warning as practical advice to run.
passages.ot:
Daniel speaks three times of this horror set up in the temple (Daniel 9:27, 11:31, and 12:11). In Daniel 11:31 an enemy's forces “will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation.” Jesus takes Daniel's words and says they are still speaking.

The great distress “unmatched from the beginning” also echoes Daniel, who speaks of “a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time” (Daniel 12:1).
passages.hard:
What exactly is the abomination? Christians have given three main answers, each with careful defenders.

Some read it as the Roman armies and the events that led to the temple's destruction in AD 70. On this view, the warning to flee was for the people of Judea in that generation, and Luke's version supports it, since Luke says, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (Luke 21:20).

Others read it as still in the future, a final enemy of God before Christ returns. Readers who hold this often link it with Paul's words about a man of lawlessness who sets himself up in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4).

Many read it both ways: fulfilled in AD 70, and also a pattern of what will come again before the end.

These notes do not choose among them. All three agree on what Jesus actually tells his followers to do: do not be fooled, do not stay to save your things, and trust God, who limits the days.
passages.asks: Jesus' advice in the crisis is surprising. He does not say stay and fight, or stay to defend the holy place. He says run, and do not go back for your things. Ask what you would cling to if you had to leave everything. Notice, too, that Jesus thinks of pregnant women and nursing mothers in the middle of a speech about the end of the world. His eye goes to the most vulnerable.

passages.t: The Son of Man coming in the clouds
passages.happening: After that distress, Jesus says, the sun will go dark, the moon will give no light, the stars will fall, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then people will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. He will send out the angels to gather his chosen people from the four winds, from one end of earth and heaven to the other.
passages.hearers:
This is the language of the prophets, and Jesus' hearers knew it. The prophets used pictures of a darkened sun and falling stars when God brought down a great power within history. Isaiah used them for the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10). A first-century Jew would not take these words as a weather report. Nor would he think they were only decoration. They meant that God was acting in a way that would shake the world.

‘Son of Man’ was Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself. Here he ties it to the figure in Daniel who comes with the clouds and receives a kingdom from God.
passages.ot:
Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.” He came to the Ancient of Days, God himself, and “He was given dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:13-14).

The gathering of God's scattered people is also an old promise. Moses told Israel that even if they were banished to the farthest horizon, “He will gather you and return you from there” (Deuteronomy 30:4). In the Old Testament, it is the LORD who gathers. Here the Son of Man sends out the angels to do it, and he calls the chosen ones his own.
passages.hard:
Does this passage describe the end of history, or the events of AD 70?

Many Christians read verses 24 to 27 as the second coming of Christ at the end of the age, when he returns in glory and gathers his people. This has been the most common reading through the centuries.

Others read the passage as describing the fall of Jerusalem in the prophets' picture-language. In Daniel, the Son of Man comes to God, not down to earth, to receive a kingdom. On this view, the temple's fall showed that Jesus had been given that kingdom. Those who read it this way still believe Christ will return, and they find that promise in verses 32 to 37 and elsewhere in the New Testament.

Still others think both are in view, the near event as a picture of the final one.

Christians who hold each of these views confess together in the creeds that Christ will come again in glory. They differ on which verses describe which event. These notes leave that question open, and they offer no end-times timetable.
passages.asks: Jesus does not end the story with falling stars. He ends it with a gathering. The last word is not chaos but his people brought home from every corner of the earth. Ask whether you think about the future mostly with fear or mostly with hope, and which one this passage invites.

passages.t: The lesson of the fig tree
passages.happening: Jesus points to a fig tree. When its branches go soft and its leaves come out, you know summer is near. In the same way, when you see these things, know that he is near, right at the door. Then he makes a solemn promise: “Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.” And he adds, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.”
passages.hearers:
Many trees in the land of Israel, such as the olive, keep their leaves all year. The fig tree does not. It stands bare through winter, and its new leaves come late. So when a fig tree put out tender leaves, everyone knew summer was close. It was a sign anyone could read.

The word ‘generation’ in Greek is genea. Every other time Mark uses it, it means the people alive in Jesus' day (8:12, 8:38, 9:19).
passages.ot: Jesus' last promise sounds like Isaiah: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Isaiah said that about the word of God. Jesus says it about his own words.
passages.hard:
Verse 30 is one of the hardest in the Bible. If ‘all these things’ includes the coming of the Son of Man, did Jesus promise that the end would come within his hearers' lifetimes? Many skeptics have said yes, and that he was wrong. The objection is serious, and Christians have felt it too. C. S. Lewis, a believer, called this saying ‘the most embarrassing verse in the Bible’ in his essay The World's Last Night.

Christians have answered in three main ways.

One reading says that ‘all these things’ means the signs and the fall of the temple, which did happen within about forty years. The coming itself is ‘that day’ in verse 32, which no one knows. Readers who hold this point out that in verse 29 ‘these things’ are signs seen before he is near, so they cannot include his coming.

A second reading says that the whole passage up to verse 30 describes AD 70, read in the prophets' picture-language, and was fulfilled within that generation.

A third reading takes ‘this generation’ in another sense, such as the generation that sees the signs, or the Jewish people, or even the kind of people who resist God.

Each view has a weakness its critics point to, and careful Christians hold each one. When Jesus will return is a question on which faithful Christians differ. That he will return is confessed by all.
passages.asks: Jesus stakes everything on his words. Heaven and earth will go, but what he has said will stand. Ask whose words you trust most when you are afraid: the news, your own feelings, or his. A fig tree teaches you to notice. Jesus wants his followers awake to what God is doing, not scanning the sky for a date.

passages.t: No one knows the day: keep watch
passages.happening: Jesus says plainly that no one knows the day or hour, “not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” So stay alert. He tells a short story. A man goes away, leaves each servant in charge of his own work, and tells the doorkeeper to keep watch. No one knows when the master will come back: in the evening, at midnight, when the rooster crows, or at dawn. Do not let him find you asleep. And then Jesus widens it to everyone: “What I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!”
passages.hearers:
A large household might have a doorkeeper whose one task was to stay awake and open the door for the master. If the master came home late at night and found him asleep, it was a failure of his whole job.

Mark names four parts of the night: evening, midnight, rooster crow, and morning. Watch for them in the next two chapters. Jesus eats the Last Supper in the evening. He prays in the garden in the night while his friends sleep. Peter denies him when the rooster crows. And in the morning Jesus is handed over to Pilate. The disciples are told to keep watch, and within hours they fall asleep.
passages.ot: Isaiah speaks of watchmen posted on the walls of Jerusalem who are never silent, day or night (Isaiah 62:6). Watching was a job, not a mood.
passages.hard:
How can the Son not know the day, if he is God? In the 300s the followers of Arius used this verse to argue that the Son was a lesser being than the Father. The church leader Athanasius answered that Jesus spoke this way as a true human being. The Son had taken on a full human life, with its real limits, as Luke says he “grew in wisdom” (Luke 2:52). The church later confessed at the Council of Chalcedon, in 451, that Christ is truly God and truly man in one person. How best to describe what Jesus knew in his earthly life is still something Christians discuss. Notice, too, that even here Jesus places himself above the angels and next to the Father.

This verse also stands against every attempt to set a date for the end. Many have tried, and every one has been wrong. If the Son did not give a date, no preacher, chart, or book can.
passages.asks: Keeping watch in this story does not mean staring at the door. It means each servant doing the work he was given while the master is away. Ask what work Jesus has given you: a family to love, a job to do honestly, a neighbor to serve. Being awake means being faithful there. If you have been frightened by end-times preaching, notice that Jesus' repeated word in this chapter is not ‘be afraid’ but ‘do not be alarmed’ and ‘keep watch’.
